newsitem.title: UK: UK venture capital funds earn 42.9% in 1996-survey.
newsitem.headline: UK venture capital funds earn 42.9% in 1996-survey.

text.p: Independent venture capital funds in the UK enjoyed a 42.9 percent net return in 1996, outpacing all other asset classes held by pension funds, according to a survey by the British Venture Capital Association (BVCA).
Venture capital funds also had five year average returns of 25.7 percent and a 10 year average of 15.7 percent, according to the survey.

"Venture capital funds' one to 10 year return out-performed all FTSE indices and all asset classes held by pension funds," said Clive Sherling, chairman of the BVCA investor relations committee and director of venture capital firm Apax Partners.

UK pension funds achieved gross returns on UK equity investment of 16.8 percent in 1996 and a 13.9 percent average over 10 years, according to The WM Company, which conducted the survey. On all assets UK pension funds made returns of 10.7 percent in 1996 and 11.9 percent average over 10 years.
The survey measured venture capital returns on a net basis, after all costs and fees, further adding to the gap in returns between venture capital and other asset classes.

The very strong 1996 returns were helped by a hot new issue market and the creation of EASDAQ, Europe's fledgling growth stocks market, both of which gave venture capital fund managers willing outlets for loss-making but fast-growing small companies, according to Sherling.
In the last two years it has become much easier to float high-technology and bio-technology companies in their development stage in the UK," Sherling said.
The overall return to independent venture capital fund investors increased to 14.2 percent per annum by the end of 1996 on funds raised between 1980 and 1992, up from 13.0 percent in 1995.

Venture capital funds raised between 1980 and 1996 have so far paid out 132 percent of investors' original capital and still retain about 39 percent of their original investment which is yet to be realised.

Funds specialising in large management buy-outs (MBO) have been by far the best performers, according to the survey. Large MBO funds, defined as those that make equity investments over 5 million sterling, had 1996 returns of 56.0 percent and average five year returns of 35.7 percent.

"We want to make venture capital like every other asset class," Sherling said. "Pension funds in the UK have less than one percent of their assets invested in venture capital, as opposed to large numbers of major pension funds in the US which have between five and 10 percent.
